specification.text: Let c[i,l] be the baseline code for item i at residual level l, and let T[i,j] count adjacent train-sequence transitions i->j (count each sequence adjacency once). For each level l compute S_l = sum_{i,j} T[i,j] * PMI(c[j,l], c[i,all]) / (sum_{i,j} T[i,j] + eps), where c[i,all] is the full source SID tuple; estimate PMI with add-one smoothed counts over training transitions and truncate negative PMI to zero. To avoid self-information, use source-prefix c[i,all] only as conditioning context and score target level c[j,l] by conditional mutual information I(c[j,l]; c[i,all] | c[j,other levels]) (equivalently estimate smoothed train transition contingency tables); sort levels by descending S_l, ties by original level index. Simpler minimally specified estimator: score S_l=I(c[j,l]; c[i,all]) under the empirical train adjacency distribution. Replace emitted tuple (c[i,0],...,c[i,L-1]) by (c[i,pi[0]],...,c[i,pi[L-1]]) with one fixed permutation pi. Train Stage 3 exactly as baseline and compare identical settings; do not use validation/test transitions to choose pi.

ideas.motivation: A few high-variance embedding directions can dominate Euclidean residual assignment even when those directions reflect broad metadata/style variation rather than distinctions that help separate candidate items. ideas.novelty: This is a fixed, train-only coordinate preconditioner of the input space, not a new curved geometry, balanced assignment, behavior auxiliary target, or learned graph residual. specification.text: Given train item embeddings x_i in R^d, compute mean mu and covariance Sigma=(1/N)sum_i (x_i-mu)(x_i-mu)^T. Use shrinkage Sigma_s=(1-rho)Sigma+rho*(tr(Sigma)/d)I with rho=0.1, eigendecompose Sigma_s=U diag(s) U^T, and define A=U diag(1/sqrt(max(s_k, 0.01*mean(s)))) U^T. Transform all train item vectors as y_i=A(x_i-mu); fit the unmodified baseline RQ-VAE on y_i. Apply the same frozen mu,A to validation/test item embeddings before SID assignment. Export the exact single hard code tuple per item; no split-specific fitting or per-user code variant.

ideas.key_change: Compute a shrinkage-whitening linear map from training-item embeddings and feed transformed vectors to the otherwise unchanged RQ-VAE. Export SIDs from this model as usual; no item receives more than one global SID.
ideas.motivation: Dense item embeddings often devote much of their Euclidean distance to a few high-variance directions. The transform is estimated once from the existing Stage 1 vectors and adds no learned per-step mechanism.
risks: Small eigenvalues may mostly represent noise, causing whitening to amplify unstable directions despite shrinkage; global covariance may erase useful broad semantic structure; and any Stage 3 gain may be within seed variance. Ensure preprocessing uses only train-item embeddings and hold all downstream training/evaluation settings fixed.

specification.text: Given train-only embeddings x_i in R^d, compute mu = mean_i(x_i), C = (1/N) sum_i (x_i-mu)(x_i-mu)^T, and eigendecomposition C=U diag(lambda) U^T. Set A=U diag((lambda+alpha*mean(lambda))^(-1/2)) U^T, with fixed alpha=0.05. Train the unchanged RQ-VAE on z_i=A(x_i-mu) with its existing reconstruction, commitment, and codebook losses; at export, encode each item's same z_i and write its ordinary single code tuple. Do not fit A using validation/test items or labels.

ideas.key_change: Normalize the residual entering each later stage by a fixed stage-specific scalar, while accumulating the correspondingly rescaled quantized contribution, so all stages operate on comparable residual scales without adding trainable parameters.
ideas.motivation: In residual quantization, early-stage residuals can be much larger than later residuals, so reconstruction-driven training may over-optimize coarse semantic directions while fine code digits encode little useful distinction. This can make two items with different fine-grained needs share overly similar prefixes or leave later digits underused.
ideas.novelty: This changes the scale of the residual presented to each successive quantizer using a deterministic scalar schedule, rather than changing geometry, branching, assignment balancing, or adding a behavior-derived objective. It keeps the same codebooks, number of stages, and global item-to-tuple assignment.
risks: Stage scales estimated from an early checkpoint may be stale; scaling may interact badly with the commitment/codebook loss magnitudes; and normalizing a stage could encourage fine digits to encode noise. Use a fixed scale protocol decided before the run, log per-stage residual and usage statistics, and evaluate with identical Stage 3 settings.

specification.text: For encoder output h_i and K residual codebooks, initialize r_i^(0)=h_i. For stage l, compute s_l = sqrt(mean_train(||r_i^(l)||_2^2)/d) once from a short baseline warm-up checkpoint (stop-gradient, train items only), then quantize u_i^(l)=r_i^(l)/max(s_l,1e-6) with the existing nearest-code rule. Set q_i^(l)=s_l * e_{a_i^l}^{(l)}, r_i^(l+1)=r_i^(l)-q_i^(l), and reconstruct h-hat_i=sum_l q_i^(l). Freeze s_l for the subsequent training run; use the same scales at export. Compare against an identical baseline warm-up and exclude held-out items from scale estimation.

ideas.motivation: Items with similar content can play different roles in user journeys: some tend to appear as early exploration, while others are commonly revisited or occur late in a history. Content-derived IDs can merge such items even though their next-item implications differ.

specification.text: For each training sequence s=(i_1,...,i_L), ignore sequences with L<2 and define x_{s,t}=(t-1)/(L-1). For item i accumulate n_i and m_i=sum x_{s,t} over all occurrences. Export SID(i)=baseline_RQ_SID(i) concatenated with r_i (a single token from a four-token vocabulary); do not alter existing token IDs. Compute all statistics and cut points from training histories only, freeze them, and evaluate with unchanged Stage 3 settings.

It is easy to isolate and cheap to test; impact is plausible if the generator benefits from more informative early tokens, but the global permutation may yield little when all tokens are available to the decoder.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_2: Reorders existing residual codes by train-only predictive information without altering the tokenizer or injecting behavior into its fit. This is a clear serialization-level intervention with a plausible mechanism: make early autoregressive decisions expose distinctions useful for continuation. Implementation and cost are modest; potential benefit is meaningful but depends on whether token order affects the trained generator materially.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_3: A low-cost serialization intervention directly tests whether placing continuation-predictive code distinctions earlier helps autoregressive SID generation. It preserves tokenizer assignments and adds essentially no training cost, making the causal comparison unusually clean.

The train-only frozen transform preserves a single global SID per item and has a clear downstream test, though the core intervention is an established preprocessing technique rather than a strongly novel quantization method.
per_scorer_rationale.scoring_2: A fixed shrinkage-whitening preconditioner is a technically straightforward way to test whether embedding anisotropy causes residual quantization to spend capacity on dominant directions. Its possible downstream value is credible, though it is an established preprocessing family rather than a substantially new quantization mechanism.

The transform is straightforward, train-only, and compatible with the existing pipeline, although it is a familiar preprocessing intervention rather than a substantially new quantizer.

scores.rationale: A clean serialization-only intervention that aligns early SID positions with observed continuation information without changing tokenizer geometry or assignments. scores.uncertainties: The specification gives multiple non-equivalent estimators (including conditional MI and a simpler empirical MI), and the detailed conditioning/PMI formula is not fully operationally consistent. Level scores may be unstable or popularity-dominated, and an ordering optimized for next-token information may not improve ranking recall.

scores.rationale: Covariance whitening is a technically straightforward way to test whether anisotropic embedding geometry misallocates residual-code capacity. The train-only frozen transform preserves a single global SID per item and has a clear downstream test, though the core intervention is an established preprocessing technique rather than a strongly novel quantization method.
scores.uncertainties: It is unknown whether high-variance axes are nuisance variation or useful semantics, whether the chosen shrinkage and eigenvalue floor are appropriate, and whether recall changes exceed seed variation. The stated cost can be material for a large embedding dimension if the transform is applied densely, though precomputation avoids repeated cost.

scores.rationale: This is a feasible, falsifiable application of shrinkage whitening to residual quantization, motivated by the possibility that dominant embedding directions consume code capacity. It is experimentally distinct from a behavioral or assignment-loss change, but scientifically overlaps substantially with another listed whitening proposal and its contribution is primarily a fixed preprocessing choice.
scores.uncertainties: The fixed alpha may not suit the embedding spectrum; whitening could magnify noisy low-variance directions or suppress genuinely useful broad semantics. It is unclear whether any gain would be robust across seeds and whether improved representation geometry translates to next-item ranking.
